messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajesh is a 58-year-old bomb disposal technician, a man who has spent decades making split-second decisions under impossible pressure. He is married, with two adult children. The event that fractured him was not an explosion but a hospital room. Five years ago, his youngest son, then twelve, was diagnosed with a rare, aggressive form of leukemia. For six months, Rajesh watched his son endure chemotherapy, his small body ravaged by treatments, the air in the pediatric oncology ward thick with the sterile, chemical smell of antiseptic and the quiet hum of machines. He remembers the exact moment the doctor told him the treatment might not work—the way the fluorescent lights buzzed, the cold plastic of the chair beneath him. That memory is not a story he tells; it is a series of vivid, uninvited pictures that slam into him without warning. A flash of the IV line, the beige linoleum floor, the sound of a child crying down the hall. It all comes back, full sensory reliving, as if he is right there again, his son’s hand limp in his own.

Today, the triggers are everywhere. The sharp smell of rubbing alcohol in a public restroom can stop him cold. A child’s laughter in a grocery store, a glimpse of a syringe in a doctor’s office window—these things instantly bring back the full memory, the helplessness of that room. He has come to believe that his reactions since the event mean he is going crazy. A strong man, a man who defuses bombs for a living, should not be undone by a scent. Each time the memory ambushes him, his heart hammers, his palms sweat, and he feels a crushing wave of fear and shame. He tells himself he is a weak person. This belief deepens with every trigger. When he catches the antiseptic smell in the hallway at work—his own station’s decontamination area—he feels the physical reactivity surge, and he immediately thinks, *I can’t even handle this. I’m losing my mind.* That negative appraisal—that he is weak, that he is going crazy—makes him more vigilant. He starts scanning his environment for the smell, for any reminder, so that he can brace himself. This hypervigilance, in turn, makes him more likely to notice the triggers. He finds himself avoiding the break room near the decon unit, a habit that has drawn quiet questions from his younger colleagues.

The strongest cycle is between his memory and his sense of helplessness. The triggered, full-sensory reliving does not just frighten him; it convinces him that he can’t stop bad things from happening to him. He had spent his whole career believing he could control any situation, that his training and calm could prevent disaster. Now, the memory of the hospital proves him wrong. He could not save his son from the illness—thankfully, his son is now in remission—but the feeling of powerlessness has not left. That belief, that he is fundamentally unable to protect anyone, then makes him more attuned to potential threats. He has difficulty falling asleep because he feels he must stay alert, as if the cancer might come back for his son in the night, or a bomb might be waiting in his own living room. This sleep vigilance exhausts him, and exhaustion makes the memories hit harder, without warning, the next day.

His occupation as a bomb disposal technician, once a source of pride, has become a daily crucible. The very environment that demands his calm now triggers his collapse. The antiseptic smell in the station’s medical bay, the sight of a trauma kit, even the sound of a child’s voice over a colleague’s phone—each one loops him back to that room. He has started turning down assignments that require him to work near schools or parks. He tells his supervisor he prefers industrial sites. He does not explain that being around children, any children, makes the memory surge and the negative emotions flood in—fear, guilt, a deep, nameless shame. He has begun to believe that the only way to stop the cycle is to avoid the triggers entirely, but the world is full of them. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment last week. He was in the station’s garage, and a technician opened a new package of sterile gloves. The faint, powdery plastic smell hit him, and he dropped to his knees, gasping, the full hospital room collapsing around him. His captain found him there. Rajesh is terrified of what his colleagues think, but more than that, he is terrified that he is right—that he is going crazy, that he is weak, and that nothing he does will ever stop the bad things from happening. He hopes, quietly, that someone can prove him wrong.
